new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (149 pp., text layer, title/author metadata match Donohue & San Roque, I'saka) and extracted PDF pp. 33-36 (printed pp. 15-18) with extracted text. All three quoted passages are present at the stated locators: p.15 end of §2.1.2 'there are two separate suprasegmental processes in I'saka, tone and nasalisation, described in the following sections'; p.16 §2.2.1 'I'saka distinguishes four pitch contrasts on single syllables. These are a High 'H' and a Low 'L' level tone, and the contour tones Rise 'R' (decomposable into LH) and Fall 'F' (decomposable into HL)'; p.17 'An alternative explanation is that tone is in fact assigned at a word level in I'saka'. Only differences are scanned spac…
new_statements.rule_in_words: I'saka is a tone language with four contrastive tones (H, L, R, F) on monosyllables; on disyllabic roots fewer than half of the 16 possible tone combinations occur, which the authors suggest may mean tone is assigned at the word level (word-tone melodies), as in related Skou, Puare, Leitre and Barupu. The grammar names tone and nasalisation as the only suprasegmental features and makes no statement about word stress or accent at all; the word 'stress' does not appear in the book.
new_statements.exceptions: None relevant to stress. Tone notes: no F on either syllable of disyllabic roots, low-low the only identical-tone sequence, high-rise unattested; a bound root's rising tone overwrites yung 'bird' F in compounds; no tonal interaction between adjacent words in a phrase (p.17).
new_statements.domain_note: Word / monomorphemic root level; too few monomorphemic words of three or more syllables to characterise longer forms (p.17). Nothing about stress in citation forms or phrases.
new_statements.identity_note: The grammar describes the language of Krisa village (Sandaun Province, PNG), called 'Krisa' in Laycock 1973/1975 and 'I'saka' by Donohue & San Roque; Glottolog kris1246 / ISO ksi cover the same variety, and the grammar states (p.10) that Laycock's 1970 'Krisa' data are lexically identical to the variety described. No dialect split is reported.

new_statements.quote: In addition to the segmental phonological units described in the previous section there are also two suprasegmental tiers, that of tone and of nasalisation, which each apply independently to the syllable. [p.16] ... I'saka distinguishes four pitch contrasts on single syllables. These are a High 'H' and a Low 'L' level tone, and the contour tones Rise 'R' (decomposable into LH) and Fall 'F' (decomposable into HL). [p.16] ... An alternative explanation is that tone is in fact assigned at a word level in I'saka: the disyllabic correlate of H is RH; that of L, LL; that of R is both LH and LR, and the correlate of F is both HL and RL ... Much more data is needed before this hypothesis can be confirmed. [p.17]

Much more data is needed before this hypothesis can be confirmed.' p.17). Read the whole of §2.2-2.2.2: only tone and nasalisation are named as suprasegmental tiers; Table 5…
new_statements.relation_note: On the identity of the variety: the archive.org item 149-isaka is not the 2002 NUS/Sydney pre-print (vii+118 pp.) that the citation names; it is the 2004 Pacific Linguistics 554 edition (xvii+131 pp., sealang.net. So it is the same text as the existing statement's source. It agrees with the existing statement (tone language, no stress statement) and adds nothing new; the 2002 pre-print itself remains unlocated online.
new_statements.rule_in_words: I'saka is a tone language with four contrastive tones on monosyllables (H, L, Rise, Fall); on disyllabic roots fewer than half the 16 possible combinations occur (no Fall in combination, LL the only identical sequence, no H-R), which the authors take as possible evidence that tone is assigned at the word level. The grammar contains no statement about word stress or accent at all: the only suprasegmental tiers named are tone and nasalisation, and a full-text search finds 'stress' nowhere (only 'distress' p.9), 'accent' only as the names of the grave/acute tone diacritics (p.38), and 'intonation' only for clause-level contours (pp.85, 95, 99).
new_statements.exceptions: None about stress. On tone: the F tone of ying 'bird' surfaces as low pitch in some compounds ([jiiru] 'forest pigeon'), taken as support for a word-based tone system; no interaction between tones of adjacent words in a phrase (p.17).
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe I'saka (= 'Krisa', named after the village), Sko family; Donohue & San Roque 2004:10 state that Laycock's 1970 'Krisa' notes are lexically the same variety. The two listed works are not distinct texts: work 0's archive.org item is the 2004 PL-554 edition, not the 2002 NUS/Sydney pre-print (vii+118 pp.) named in the citation, and work 1's HathiTrust item is the same 2004 edition (ISBN 9780858835542) despite Glottolog's 2002 date. The 2002 pre-print itself has not been located online.

sources.note: Chapter 2 Phonology (pp.13-37) lists exactly two suprasegmental processes, tone and nasalisation (§2.2, p.15-16); I'saka has four contrastive tones H, L, R, F on monosyllables (§2.2.1, p.16), possibly assigned at word level (p.17). The word 'stress' does not occur anywhere in the book (a full-text search for stress/accent; only 'distress' p.9); no accent/prominence statement at all.
